Description
Cal Poly Humboldt’s Department of Wildlife seeks a master’s student to study barn owl nest-site selection in California almond and pistachio orchards. Fieldwork in the southern Central Valley in late spring/early summer 2027 and 2028 will involve monitoring 64 new camera-equipped nest boxes, half containing debris from previously used barn owl boxes, to test whether barn owls use social cues when selecting nest sites. The student will also help capture and age colonizing owls and fit as many as possible with GPS trackers. The position runs from January 2027 through December 2028 and pays $33,280 annually for 20 hours/week during the academic year, while also taking classes, and 40 hours/week during summer (@$26/hr). An in-state tuition waiver worth approximately $11,000/year is also included. Applicants from the 15 Western States receive the full waiver; those from other states are responsible for out-of-state tuition, currently $396/unit.

The position will also involve supervising one field technicians to assist with field work. The work is funded by the California Dept of Pesticide Regulation and will involve collaboration with Drs. Danny Karp and Roger Baldwin from UC Davis’s Dept of Wildlife, Fish, and Conservation Biology.

Required qualifications include: (a) BS in Ecology, Wildlife or related field, (b) interest in and capacity for technical aspects of camera traps and GPS tags, (c) strong quantitative skills, (d) interest in agroecology, and (e) willingness to work in hot conditions and in collaboration with private farms. Preferred qualifications include experience handling raptors, experience with statistical modeling analyses using R, and/or experience working with farmers. 

Candidates should express interest with a cover letter/statement of purpose, resume, and list of three references in an email to Matt Johnson at matt.johnson@humboldt.edu; please use the subject line OWL SOCIAL CUE MS APPLICANT. Your application statement of purpose should express interest in this position and articulate the required and any preferred qualifications. The top selected candidate will then be asked to fully apply to the Natural Resources graduate program at Cal Poly Humboldt https://cnrs.humboldt.edu/node/294. In addition to the application documents already mentioned, the full graduate school application also requires official transcripts and a $70 application fee.

Applications accepted now (Sept 2026); review of applicants begins on 30 Oct 2026; the position remains open until filled.

Description
 Program Title & Department: Towson University, Environmental Science and Studies Program (ENVS). More information about the program is available here: (https://www.towson.edu/fcsm/departments/environsci/), and graduate program-specific information is available here: (https://www.towson.edu/fcsm/departments/environsci/grad/). 

The Project: The Kraskura Ecological Fish Physiology Lab in the Fisher College of Science & Mathematics at Towson University is leading a new study funded by the Chesapeake Bay Trust on the impacts of stream restoration on fish physiological performance, habitat suitability, and distributions. The objectives for the Master’s thesis are to i) monitor physiological bioindicators (lipid content, oxidative stress markers, and body condition) in common stream fish species across the restoration timeline and across sites with different restoration levels, and to ii) characterize the effects of temperature and conductivity on fish swimming and aerobic capacity. These data will support habitat suitability modeling and help evaluate the success of stream restoration projects. 

The Lab: We value an encouraging, safe environment where everyone deserves to learn and participate fully. We work as a team and integrate undergraduate students in our research. You can read more about our lab: https://kraskura.github.io/ 

Financial Support & Funding: This project is fully funded as a Research Assistantship, including full tuition remission and a stipend (avg $21.5 K per year, benefits not included) for 2 years. If needed, support may be extended with a Teaching or Research Assistantship through the ENVS program. Because the student is expected to present findings at scientific conferences, travel will be supported through internal funding or project funds. 

Essential Skills to Successfully Complete the Project: 
A strong candidate should have prior experience working with live animals, be comfortable in laboratory and field settings, and demonstrate strong project management skills. The experiences and abilities essential for this project are outlined below. The candidate must have a driver’s license and the ability to drive a work vehicle to and from field sites. 
Work in the field (fish surveys, field dissections) 
Work with live fish in an animal facility (e.g., animal care, experimental procedures, dissections) 
Work in the laboratory (e.g., pipetting) 
Effective communication skills (e.g., with external partners, internal collaborators, undergraduate student researchers) 
Excellent organization and data management skills (e.g., tracking large numbers of samples, data entry) 
Team management skills (e.g., coordinating field trips, assembling team, task allocation and management) 
Experience with data and statistical analysis using R (or another similar program like Python). 
Strong writing skills (e.g., writing a manuscript for peer review in a scientific journal; standard operating procedures). 

Important Dates: 
Email application to Dr. Kraskura: October 1, 2026. 
The application to the ENVS program: November 1, 2026. 
Start of the program: Spring 2027 (January 25, 2027) 

Interested applicants should submit a one-page cover letter describing their relevant past experience, motivation to pursue a graduate degree, and reasons for applying to this position, along with a CV or resume and contact information for three professional references, via e-mail to Dr. Krista Kraskura (kkraskura@towson.edu) by October 1. Qualified and competitive applicants will be invited to video-interview with Dr. Kraskura, and competitive applicants will be invited to submit their applications to the Environmental Science and Studies Program (ENVS). Application details can be found: https://www.towson.edu/fcsm/departments/environsci/grad/science/admission.html.

kkraskura@towson.edu (preferred contact method)

Program Title & Department: Biological Sciences Program or Environmental Science and Studies Program (ENVS), Thesis Track, Towson University. Program details and admission requirements for each program: Biological Sciences and ENVS.

Project Description: The Kraskura Lab in the Fischer College of Natural Sciences at Towson University is leading an innovative new study funded by the Chesapeake Bay Trust on the impacts of stream restoration in the Chesapeake Bay on fish performance, habitat suitability, and distributions. Data collection prior to the student’s start date will include in situ sampling of fish and stream conditions at sites with different restoration levels, followed by laboratory experiments to assess fish aerobic scope and swimming capacity. A highly motivated student is sought to utilize this data to create a mechanistic habitat suitability model, with results relayed in maps and provided to collaborators and stakeholders in an interactive format (e.g., R Shiny Application). The student is also expected to publish their thesis work in a reputable and appropriate journal within a timely manner of thesis completion.

Financial Support, Funding, and Mentorship: This project is fully funded as a Research Assistantship, including full tuition remission and a stipend (avg $21.5 K per year, benefits not included) for 2 years. If needed, support may possibly be extended with a Teaching Assistantship. Because the student is expected to present preliminary results and final findings at scientific conferences, travel will be supported through internal funding or project funds.  The student will be primarily mentored by PI Dr Krista Kraskura, a fish physiologist who will provide training on integrative methods (e.g., field, lab, and quantitative) for studying fish physiology, and will have co-mentorship from Dr Nicki Barbour, a spatial and movement ecologist with expertise in statistical modeling and mapping in R. Both the Kraskura and Barbour labs value an encouraging and safe environment, where everyone deserves to learn and participate in full. You can read more about Dr. Kaskura’s lab here and about Dr. Barbour’s work here.

Essential Skills: The competitive candidate for this position will have strong skills in statistical modeling of ecological data, preferably with explicit experience in habitat suitability modeling and creating maps in R. The ideal candidate is also expected to have foundational understandings of fish ecology, physiology, and aquatic environments and to have excellent written and oral communication skills. 

Application Details:

1.        Email application to Dr. Barbour: October 15, 2026.
2.        The application deadline, if applying to the ENVS program: January 15, 2027.
3.        The application deadline, if applying to the Biological Sciences program: November 15, 2026.
4.        Start of the program: Fall 2027

Interested applicants should submit a one-page cover letter describing their relevant past experience, motivation to pursue a graduate degree, and reasons for applying to this position, as well as a CV or resume, and contact information for three professional references via e-mail to Dr Nicki Barbour (nbarbour@towson.edu).  Qualified and competitive applicants will be invited to conduct video interviews with Dr. Kraskura and Dr Barbour, and competitive applicants will be invited to submit their applications to the best fitting Master’s program. 

Contact
Nicole Barbour
nbarbour@towson.edu (preferred contact method)

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), in Corvallis, Oregon.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: You will assist in research into the genetics of heat and drought tolerance in perennial ryegrass in field and lab settings under the guidance of a mentor at the Forage Seed and Cereal Research Unit in Corvallis, OR. In the field, you will help collect and analyze trait measurements related to plant development, plant physiology, and seed yield under different irrigation regimes in two locations with different weather patterns. You will also aid in conducting a Genome Wide Association Study to identify genetic variants associated with these traits. In the lab, you will help evaluate root growth under heat and drought conditions and develop mapping populations to identify genes contributing to specific growth patterns.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will develop skills or learn about:

Research strategies unique to obligate outcrossing grass species
Measuring traits associated with plant development, physiology, and seed yield
Genetics and genomics approaches to marker-trait associations
Effective scientific communication and collaboration
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Joseph Gallagher (joseph.gallagher@usda.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: Fall 2026. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email ORISE.ARS.PacificWest@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should have received a doctoral degree in one of the relevant fields. Degree must have been received within the past five years.

Preferred skills:

Experience with plant genetics
Experience with plant abiotic stress research
Experience with field, greenhouse, and laboratory research

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: The USDA-ARS Food Science & Market Quality and Handling Research Unit is engaged in the development of new and enhanced technologies that support vegetable pickling, by fermentation or acidification, in the USA, under the USDA-ARS National Program 306, Quality and Utilization of Agricultural Products. A current research project evaluates the role of microbes in texture losses of vegetables during processing and long-term storage. You will participate in all aspects of scientific research and laboratory operations with specific and expanded opportunities associated with microscopy using a Keyence Imaging System, enzyme kinetic assays using microbial cultures, supernatants and/or extracts, and texture measurements on vegetable tissue. You will participate in data collection and analysis and collaboratively advance the development of standard operating procedures for advanced microscopy.

Learning Objectives: Through this educational opportunity, you will develop foundational knowledge and practical skills in the following areas:

Master routine laboratory techniques to ensure the production of accurate and reproducible data, along with the ability to collect, process, and analyze such data effectively.
Build proficiency in microscopy techniques and microbial enzyme assays, enhancing understanding of microbial processes.
Learn methods for measuring food texture, with a specific focus on vegetables, to explore applications in food science.
This experience is designed to foster growth in scientific understanding and technical expertise within a supportive learning environment.

I am looking for a new doctoral student in my Aquatic Ecology lab for Fall 2027 (North Miami, FL). I am looking for a curious independent thinker who is honest, hard-working and motivated to study populations or communities in aquatic ecosystems, specifically in wetlands. The PhD project may involve use of long-term data collected on federal and state-funded monitoring projects.  Dissertation topics are partly at the discretion of the student, but some aspect should involve population ecology, invasive fish ecology or trophic interactions of aquatic animals or wading birds in the context of wetland environmental variation (droughts, floods, nutrients).  The immediate context of our work is the Everglades wetland of southern Florida.  (Current PhD students are studying population dynamics and predator-prey interactions in food webs of temporary wetlands).
 The position will be supported each year with a combination of research and teaching assistantship (annual stipend of $30,625 plus a tuition waiver and health benefits) with opportunities to apply for fellowships in later years.   It may be possible that the position could start earlier in the summer (May-June) as a technician before matriculation. 
    Qualifications: 
The positions require a bachelor’s degree in biology plus extensive research experience or a completed MS degree in a related field.  A demonstrated strong work ethic and the ability to conduct field work and data analyses will both be important. The student will become part of a large lab (students, postdocs and technicians) and therefore having the ability to both work in a team and independently will be required. Previous scientific writing experience is important. An MS degree and prior research experience with ecology and/or work in wetlands are desirable.  Minimum academic qualifications include an undergraduate GPA > 3.0 three letters of recommendation. A GRE is helpful, but not required. A valid driver's license is required.  
 Interested students should send their materials to Dr. Nathan Dorn (ndorn@fiu.edu) before officially applying to the PhD program at FIU (https://case.fiu.edu/biology/phd-in-biology/admissions/index.html).

Description
A PhD position is available at Auburn University, with a start date of May 2027 or earlier. The
student will join Ian Butts’ Reproductive Physiology Lab in the School of Fisheries, Aquaculture
and Aquatic Sciences (SFAAS). Our long-term research goals are to support the development
of sustainable aquaculture, fisheries management, and conservation biology. We use an
interdisciplinary approach to investigate reproduction and hatchery science in aquatic organisms,
with a particular focus on understanding and controlling biological processes that influence
offspring performance and production.
Responsibilities and Tasks
Hybrid catfish production (blue catfish
males × channel catfish females) is an
important sector of U.S. aquaculture, but
producing high-quality sperm from blue
catfish remains a major challenge. This
project will investigate the physiological
and molecular mechanisms underlying
gamete quality and reproductive
performance, with the goal of improving
fertilization and early offspring production.
The student will spend approximately 75%
of their time conducting laboratory research
and 25% conducting pond-based research.
Research opportunities will include:
o Predicting and improving sperm quality
for in vitro fertilization
o Developing gamete quality biomarkers using multi-omics analyses (see Fig.)
o Understanding the reproductive physiology of blue catfish
o Developing new approaches to improve reproductive performance in hybrid catfish
The student will gain hands-on experience with biochemical, endocrine, molecular biology,
cellular, and functional omics techniques, while addressing research questions directly relevant to
the aquaculture industry.
Qualifications
We are looking for a motivated and enthusiastic candidate with:
o Master’s degree in biology, aquaculture, fisheries, or a closely related field
o Interest in aquaculture, molecular physiology, and reproductive biology
o Laboratory experience in molecular biology and/or physiology
o Experience with bioinformatics is an asset
o Practical experience with fish husbandry or aquatic organisms is an asset
o Strong communication, teamwork, and problem-solving skills
o Ability to obtain a U.S. driver’s license and have access to a vehicleApproval and Enrollment
The graduate appointment is subject to academic approval, and the successful candidate will be
enrolled in the PhD program within the School of Fisheries, Aquaculture and Aquatic Sciences
(SFAAS).
Salary and Appointment Terms
The project will be based at the E.W. Shell Fisheries Center in Auburn, Alabama, with additional
research conducted at universities and research facilities in the Midwestern United States. The PhD
appointment provides a $30,000 annual salary plus fringe benefits for four years. A tuition waiver
is typically provided. The student will begin coursework and research in May 2027.
Application
Please submit your application by February 1, 2027, at 11:59 PM CST.
Applications should be emailed to iab0007@auburn.edu as one PDF file containing all application
materials:
o Cover letter/motivation letter (1–2 pages) describing your background, research interests,
and career goals
o Curriculum vitae, including e-mail addresses and phone numbers for three referees
o Unofficial transcripts and GRE scores (see GRE information)
For further information about the project, please contact Dr. Ian A.E. Butts at iab0007@auburn.edu

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agriculture Research Service (ARS), located at Temple, Texas.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

The Grassland, Soil & Water Research Laboratory in Temple, TX conducts research on how to improve agronomic and economic efficiencies for row crops and grazing lands that will also reduce the producer's environmental impact. This opportunity is in support of the Conservation Effects Assessment Project that evaluates conservation practices with special emphasis on water quality and soil health. 

Research Project: During this fellowship, you will have the opportunity to be involved in research that supports the Conservation Effects Assessment Project that evaluates conservation practices in row crops and grazinglands with special emphasis on water quality and soil health. You will gain knowledge of common field and laboratory experimental procedures and how to operate equipment in both the field and lab environment. Under the guidance of a mentor, you will have the opportunity to participate in field research that may include collecting soil, plant or water samples, making treatments for field experiments (e.g., planting seed or applying fertilizer). Field equipment may include tractors, planters and hay equipment. Please note that field research may occur during adverse weather (e.g., extreme heat or cold, during rainfall events). Laboratory activities may include processing soil, plant or water samples for analysis, performing standardized analyses or running laboratory equipment to analyze chemical constituents of soil, plant and water samples. 

Learning objectives: During this opportunity, under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Learn how conservation practices in row-crop and grazingland systems affect water quality and soil health.
Gain hands-on experience with common field and laboratory experimental procedures used in agricultural and environmental research.
Develop skills in collecting soil, plant, and water samples under field conditions.
Learn to establish and maintain field experiments, including planting seed, applying fertilizer, and implementing other experimental treatments.
Become familiar with agricultural field equipment, including tractors, planters, hay equipment, and precision-agriculture monitoring systems.
Gain experience researching safely and effectively in varied field conditions, including heat, cold, and rainfall events.
Learn how precision-agriculture data are collected, managed, and used to support research in conservation practices.
Develop laboratory skills for processing soil, plant, and water samples for chemical and physical analysis.
Gain experience conducting standardized laboratory analyses and operating instruments that measure chemical constituents in environmental and agricultural samples.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Douglas Smith (douglas.r.smith@usda.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: October 2026. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors. 

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for six months, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

Experience operating farm equipment (e.g., tractors, planters, hay equipment, etc.,) and/or laboratory equipment (spectrometers, gas chromatograph, etc.,).

 ARS Office/Lab and Location: A postdoctoral research opportunity is available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), Corn Insects and Crop Genetics Research Unit, Ames, Iowa, and National Center for Agricultural Utilization Research, Peoria, Illinois.  

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS delivers cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence. 

ARS’s SCINet/Artificial Intelligence (AI) Center of Excellence Research Participation Program offers research opportunities to motivated postdoctoral fellows interested in solving agriculture-related problems at a range of spatial and temporal scales, from the genome to the continent, and sub-daily to evolutionary time scales. One of the goals of the SCINet Initiative is to develop and apply new technologies, including AI and machine learning (ML), to help solve complex agricultural problems that also depend on collaboration across scientific disciplines and geographic locations. In addition, many of these technologies rely on the synthesis, integration, and analysis of large, diverse datasets that benefit from high-performance computing (HPC). The objective of these fellowships is to facilitate cross-disciplinary, cross-location research through collaborative research on problems of interest to each applicant and amenable to or requiring HPC resources. Training will be provided in data science, scientific computing, AI/ML, and related topics as needed for the fellow to complete their research. Additional funds are available for supplies and travel essential for the fellow's research. 

Research Project: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will participate in research on interactions between maize and agriculturally important fungal pathogens, initially emphasizing Fusarium and Aspergillus species. These fungi cause crop diseases and mycotoxin contamination, reducing agricultural productivity, grain quality, and food and feed safety. The research will integrate genome sequences, genetic variation, transcriptomic profiles, functional annotations, protein structures, molecular networks, and disease-resistance phenotypes. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and bioinformatics will connect genotypes with phenotypes and identify maize and fungal genes, alleles, variants, and genomic loci influencing disease resistance, pathogen virulence, toxin production, and host recognition. 

You will have the opportunity to participate in the development and application of foundation models for fungal DNA and protein sequences. With ARS and external AI knowledge-holders, you will adapt long-context DNA language models to fungal genomes. These DNA-language models will support genome-wide prediction of variant effects across pathogen populations represented in USDA-ARS culture collections. Simultaneously, protein language models and structural methods will evaluate protein variation and predict maize–fungal protein interactions, connecting host and pathogen variation with disease outcomes and targeted disease- and mycotoxin-control strategies. 

Learning Objectives: Under mentor guidance, you will develop experience in host–pathogen genomics by integrating crop and pathogen variation, gene expression, functional annotations, protein information, and disease-resistance phenotypes. You will gain experience applying AI, genomics, and bioinformatics, from foundational AI/ML concepts to hands-on application and optimization of DNA and protein language models, including models customized for fungal genomes. 

Training will include crop and fungal RNA-seq analysis; integration of multi-omic and phenotypic data; protein-interaction and structure-based analyses; and population and comparative genomics to examine genetic diversity, selection, pangenome relationships, and functional conservation. You will also develop reproducible GPU- and CPU-based high-performance computing pipelines and package models and analytical methods as documented, reusable research software and community resources. 

You will be encouraged to participate in SCINet and AI Center of Excellence training, meetings, seminars, and professional-development activities. Opportunities may include contributing to scientific groups and collaborating with students and researchers applying computational genomics and AI methods. 

USDA-ARS Mentor: If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact Carson Andorf (carson.andorf@usda.gov) and Hye-Seon Kim (hyeseon.kim@usda.gov).

Level of Participation: The appointment is full-time. 

Participant Stipend: The participant(s) will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience. The current stipend range for this opportunity is $100,000 - $110,000/year plus a supplement to offset health insurance costs. Funding is also available to help offset relocation costs, if applicable.

Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

EPA Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention (OCSPP), with the Andrew W. Breidenbach Environmental Research Center located in Cincinnati, Ohio.

The mission of EPA is to protect human health and the environment. EPA works to ensure that: Americans have clean air, land and water; National efforts to reduce environmental risks are based on the best available scientific information; Federal laws protecting human health and the environment are administered and enforced fairly, effectively and as Congress intended; Environmental stewardship is integral to U.S. policies concerning natural resources, human health, economic growth, energy, transportation, agriculture, industry, and international trade, and these factors are similarly considered in establishing environmental policy; All parts of society have access to accurate information sufficient to effectively participate in managing human health and environmental risks; Contaminated lands and toxic sites are cleaned up; and chemicals in the marketplace are reviewed for safety.

Research Project: Due to the large number of chemicals in commerce and subsequently introduced into the environment, chemical safety assessments based on traditional animal testing have been unable to keep pace with the need to generate hazard information to support screening, prioritization, and both human health and ecological risk assessment. To address this, EPA's Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention is developing and evaluating alternative testing approaches (termed "new approach methodologies") for generating toxicity information in a more rapid and cost-effective manner while still providing data that are equivalent to or better than that derived from traditional testing. EPA's Risk Assessment Support Division is developing and applying high throughput test methods in which small aquatic organisms (e.g., embryo-larval fish, crustaceans, insect larva, aquatic plants and algae) are exposed to test chemicals. To further the interpretation of the results, you may also be engaged in literature review and hypothesis-driven studies that help establish causal relationships between perturbation of biological systems at the molecular and cellular level and adverse effects on individuals and/or populations. 

With guidance from the mentor, you may be involved in any or all of the following training activities:
Conducting laboratory exposures to organic chemicals using aquatic organisms including fish, invertebrates, and algae. 
Extracting biomolecules including DNA, RNA, endogenous metabolites, etc. from animal and plant tissues.
Conducting molecular, biochemical, physiological, and/or histological analyses on biofluids and tissue samples collected from aquatic organisms. 
Screening chemicals or chemical mixtures for biological activity using a diversity of cell-free, cell-based, and/or high throughput testing approaches.
Applying computational pipelines, bioinformatic approaches, statistical analyses, and quality assurance/quality control principles to complex biological data sets including those from "omics" technologies.
Compiling and summarizing scientific information from the peer-reviewed literature and from on-line data sources.
Conducting critical weight of evidence-based evaluations based on Bradford Hill considerations.
Analyzing experimental data and generating tables, figures, and other summaries of results.
Presenting research results at scientific meetings and contributing to peer-reviewed publications.
Learning Objectives: Through this appointment, you will:

Learn a diversity of laboratory techniques which can be applied across life sciences research fields.
Learn to operate and use a range of scientific equipment.  
Learn to engage with aquatic organisms, cell culture, and/or biochemical assays.
Learn search strategies and tools to efficiently and transparently document literature retrieval and evaluation.
Learn to evaluate data quality, trouble shoot research results, apply statistical methods for data analysis and interpretation.
You will be participating alongside a transdisciplinary research team and engage in multiple aspects of project planning, communication, research implementation, and analysis. You will be afforded an opportunity to interact with internationally recognized leaders, both within and outside EPA. Additionally, you will have the opportunity to contribute to original research and associated publications. It is expected that this training opportunity will provide you with knowledge, skills, and abilities needed to apply new technologies and associated data to regulatory decision-making at the local, national, and/or international scale and to a professional career in life sciences research.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Adam Biales (biales.adam@epa.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor.

Participants do not become employees of EPA, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

ORISE offers all ORISE EPA graduate students and Postdocs a free 5-year membership to the National Postdoctoral Association (NPA).

The successful applicant(s) will be required to comply with Environmental, Safety and Health (ES&H) requirements of the hosting facility. 

Questions: Please see the FAQ section of our website. If you have additional questions about the application process, please email ORISE.EPA.Other@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

The qualified candidate should have received a bachelor's or master's degree in one of the relevant fields (e.g. biology, (eco)toxicology, biochemistry, molecular biology, genetics, bioinformatics, computational biology, computational chemistry, chemistry, or a related field). Degree must have been received within the past five years. Those currently pursuing a master's degree are also eligible to apply.

Training or experience in organic chemistry, biochemistry, and analytical chemistry.

The Severud Wildlife Ecology Lab at South Dakota State University (SDSU) is seeking a highly motivated PhD student to study Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep population ecology and restoration in the Greater Badlands ecosystem of South Dakota.


Bighorn sheep in and around Badlands National Park experienced a severe respiratory disease outbreak beginning in 2021, resulting in substantial adult mortality, prolonged recruitment failure, and an estimated 80% population decline. Following several years of intensive disease surveillance and management, Badlands National Park and its partners are transitioning from disease management to active population recovery.


A major component of this recovery effort will be augmentation of the population with bighorn sheep from disease-free source populations. The successful applicant will have the unusual opportunity to begin a PhD at the outset of this large-scale restoration effort and evaluate how resident and translocated bighorn sheep respond to population augmentation.


Research


The PhD project will focus broadly on the demographic and ecological response of bighorn sheep to population augmentation and recovery. The student will work with GPS/VHF telemetry, population surveys, recruitment monitoring, mortality investigations, GIS data, and existing long-term datasets.


Potential research topics include:


·         Survival and causes of mortality of resident and translocated bighorn sheep


·         Post-translocation movements, establishment, and integration with resident subherds


·         Habitat use and factors associated with successful establishment


·         Reproduction, lamb recruitment, and population growth


·         Demographic responses to augmentation


·         Development of monitoring and analytical approaches to inform future augmentation and long-term bighorn sheep management


The project will also include continued disease surveillance and collection of biological samples that may support complementary genetic or other analyses. These activities are important components of the broader restoration program but are not intended to prescribe separate dissertation chapters.


Specific dissertation questions will be developed collaboratively by the student, SDSU, National Park Service, and project partners based on the student’s interests, available data, and management needs.



Collaboration and Fieldwork


This is a highly collaborative and applied project involving South Dakota State University, Badlands National Park, South Dakota Department of Game, Fish and Parks, Oglala Sioux Parks and Recreation Authority, and other state, Tribal, federal, and academic partners.


The student will participate in bighorn sheep capture and translocation activities, telemetry and population monitoring, mortality investigations, data management and analysis, and communication of results to project partners. The student will work closely with experienced agency biologists and field personnel while taking the lead on research and analyses contributing to their dissertation.



Qualifications


Applicants should have:


·         An M.S. degree in wildlife ecology, biology, natural resources, or a closely related field by the anticipated start date


·         Experience conducting wildlife field research


·         Strong interest in wildlife population ecology, quantitative ecology, and applied conservation


·         Experience with R and statistical analysis, or demonstrated potential and interest in developing strong quantitative skills


·         Strong written and oral communication skills


·         Ability to work independently and collaboratively with a diverse group of project partners


·         Ability and willingness to conduct fieldwork under challenging conditions


·         A valid driver’s license


Experience with GPS/VHF telemetry, ungulates, wildlife capture and handling, survival or demographic analysis, GIS/spatial analysis, or population modeling is desirable but not required. Applicants are not expected to have experience in all of these areas.


We are particularly interested in candidates who combine scientific curiosity, quantitative potential, field experience, strong communication skills, and an interest in conducting research that directly informs wildlife conservation and management.



Funding and Timing


The anticipated start date is January 2027. The project is being developed as a four-year PhD research and restoration project, with graduate stipend, tuition support, research expenses, field support, and professional travel incorporated into the funding structure. Final funding and administrative agreements are currently being completed.



About the Severud Wildlife Ecology Lab


The Severud Wildlife Ecology Lab is housed in the Department of Natural Resource Management at South Dakota State University in Brookings, South Dakota. Our lab conducts applied wildlife research in close collaboration with state, federal, and Tribal partners, with particular interests in ungulate ecology, population dynamics, wildlife disease, and wildlife conservation and management.


More information about the lab and SDSU’s graduate program can be provided upon request.



How to Apply


Interested applicants should email a single PDF containing:


1.      A cover letter describing your research interests, relevant experience, and interest in this project


2.      Curriculum vitae


3.      Unofficial undergraduate and graduate transcripts


4.      Contact information for three professional references


In your cover letter, please describe your experience with wildlife field research and quantitative analysis and identify the aspects of this project that most interest you.

Job Description
Tenure-track faculty position (open-rank tenure track position) with the Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute (CKWRI) in the Department of Rangeland and Wildlife Sciences (RWSC) and Dick and Mary Lewis Kleberg College of Agriculture and Natural Resources at Texas A&M University-Kingsville. This endowed chair position includes expectations of developing an extramurally funded research program focused on quail ecology and management (75%), teaching 1 graduate and 1 undergraduate level course (25%), and will be a 9-month appointment with potential for summer salary. We seek an accomplished scholar to lead an impactful and dynamic quail and upland gamebird research program, contribute to undergraduate and graduate student academic growth using the best practices in teaching and mentorship, and extend results to stakeholders, society, and the scientific community. The Glassell Chair in Quail Research will work closely with faculty including other upland gamebird scientists at CKWRI and will have access to a variety of resources to support quail research. Initial salary shall be commensurate with qualifications and experience.

Essential Duties and Responsibilities
Research 
Develop and lead an impactful, dynamic, and extramurally funded quail and upland gamebird research program, with a focus in Texas commensurate with a 75% research appointment.
Engage in scholarly activities appropriate to the discipline, contributing to the university’s research mission.

Teaching
 Teach 1 graduate-level and 1 undergraduate-level course annually 
Maintain high standards of teaching effectiveness and student engagement.

Service
 Mentor graduate and undergraduate students in research and professional development.
Engage in professional service within the Department, College, and University.

Qualifications
Applicants must have earned a Ph.D. in ecology, wildlife science, rangeland science, or closely related field from an accredited university. 
Evidence of innovative and applied research within wildlife or rangeland sciences, quail/upland gamebird management and ecology, ornithology, or ecology demonstrated by a record of producing manuscripts, presentations, and other scholarly materials. 
A dedication to teaching and the ability to instruct courses in wildlife and rangeland ecology and management, incorporating new technologies and teaching techniques into classes. Applicants must have successfully completed a minimum of 18 graduate-level hours in wildlife and rangeland science or similar disciplines related to ecosystem management. 
Demonstrated potential to attract extramural funding. 
Demonstrated ability to communicate with students, professionals, lay audiences, and other scientists. 

Preferred Qualifications
Experience conducting research on upland gamebirds in working landscapes. 
Strong quantitative skills. 
Demonstrated ability to foster and sustain positive, working relationships with private landowners, other faculty, students, and state, federal, tribal, and private natural resource organizations. 
Postdoctoral experience which may include University teaching and research. 

Knowledge, Skills and Abilities
 Strong ability to communicate research findings through peer-reviewed publications, presentations, and via media contributions 
Ability to build and sustain a nationally recognized research program through grantsmanship, graduate student recruitment and mentoring, and a strong professional presence. 
Ability to engage with diverse stakeholders (e.g., private landowners, agency personnel) in South Texas and beyond 
Ability to positively and professionally interact with students, faculty, and staff 
Skilled in using various learning strategies to maintain teaching effectiveness 
Ability to advise, mentor, and guide students to promote student success 

Additional Information
 This position is security sensitive 
This position will require export-control authorization prior to starting employment. 
This position requires compliance with state and federal laws/codes and Texas A&M University System/TAMU policies, regulations, rules and procedures 
All tasks and job responsibilities must be performed safely without injury to self or others in compliance with System and University safety requirements

How to Apply
Qualified applicants should submit a (1) cover letter, (2) a statement of teaching and research philosophies, (3) detailed vita stating education, experience, and qualifications, (4) copies of transcripts from all colleges attended, and (5) three professional references including names, e-mail addresses, and telephone numbers.
Submit applications here
Address referrals and questions regarding the position to Dr. Jennifer Smith (Jennifer.Smith@tamuk.edu)

Application Deadline: 6 November, 2026 or until a qualified candidate is identified. Preferred start date is June 2027, but start date is negotiable

Description
ARS Office/Lab and Location: A postdoctoral research opportunity is available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), Virus and Prion Research Unit, National Animal Disease Center, Ames, Iowa. 

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS delivers cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence. 

ARS’s SCINet/Artificial Intelligence (AI) Center of Excellence Research Participation Program offers research opportunities to motivated postdoctoral fellows interested in solving agriculture-related problems at a range of spatial and temporal scales, from the genome to the continent, and sub-daily to evolutionary time scales. One of the goals of the SCINet Initiative is to develop and apply new technologies, including AI and machine learning (ML), to help solve complex agricultural problems that also depend on collaboration across scientific disciplines and geographic locations. In addition, many of these technologies rely on the synthesis, integration, and analysis of large, diverse datasets that benefit from high-performance computing (HPC). The objective of these fellowships is to facilitate cross-disciplinary, cross-location research through collaborative research on problems of interest to each applicant and amenable to or requiring HPC resources. Training will be provided in data science, scientific computing, AI/ML, and related topics as needed for the fellow to complete their research. Additional funds are available for supplies and travel essential for the fellow's research.

Research Project: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will apply computational methods for identifying predictors and facilitators of immune protection against highly virulent strains of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome viruses (PRRSVs) that have recently emerged and caused high morbidities and mortalities in United States swine herds. Efforts may result in identifying novel biological targets for more effective PRRSV prevention and treatment strategies that modulate early host immune responses. During this training opportunity, you will have the opportunity to be involved in the development of a training model to predict PRRSV disease outcomes in field-collected samples from pigs infected with unknown PRRSV strains and present a portfolio of biomarkers, cell populations, and/or immune processes to target for revised immunomodulatory design strategies that are catered towards prevention/treatment of diverse PRRSV strains causing extreme pathogenesis and disease. Transcriptomics datasets have been generated via bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing from blood and disease-affected tissues and will be analyzed alongside clinical readouts and additional laboratory assay measures of disease to generate novel tools and resources for PRRSV control strategies that benefit United States pork producers.

You will also be a member of a scientific team that advances a comprehensive research program in virology, immunology, and computational biology to develop solutions for protecting United States swine herds from viral disease threats. Research endeavors are intrinsically collaborative and foster synergistic relationships with scientists across multiple ARS research institutions/national programs, academic institutions, and research consortiums. Uniquely, you will also have collaborative interactions with the ultimate targeted audience of their research: swine industry stakeholders, such as practicing swine veterinarians, pork producers, and members of the veterinary biologics industry.

Learning Objectives: During this appointment, you will learn to: a) handle multiple bulk and single-cell transcriptomics datasets through established and newly developed computational pipelines to identify patterns of gene expression, cell populations, and immune processes; and b) evaluate additional clinical, blood, and tissue sample data collected longitudinally across the post-infection study time course to optimize machine learning methods that predict disease outcomes and identify host factors and interactions that most heavily influence outcomes based on early immune response dynamics. Opportunities for additional training, communication of findings, and professional networking will also be available.

Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Jayne Wiarda (jayne.wiarda@usda.gov), Research Microbiologist at the National Animal Disease Center. If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor.

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: Targeted start date is between December 2026 to May 2027. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors. 

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year but may be renewed for a second year upon recommendation of the mentor and ARS. 

Level of Participation: The appointment is full-time. 

Participant Stipend: The participant(s) will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience. The current stipend range for this opportunity is $100,000 - $110,000/year plus a supplement to offset health/dental insurance costs. Funding is also available to help offset relocation costs, if applicable. Funds will also be available for travel to present research. 

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE. 

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email ORISE.ARS.SCINet@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received a doctoral degree in the one of the relevant fields.

Preferred Skills:

Awareness of the biological relevancy of and applications for developed computational models and workflows
Experience analyzing host/eukaryote RNA sequencing data

The USGS Great Lakes Science Center’s Oswego Biological Station (Oswego, NY) is hiring a full-time (40 hours/week), 12-month Student Contractor position to assist with fisheries research. We are looking for a recently graduated (within the last 12-months) individual who is excited to work collaboratively as part of a team. This is an excellent position for an individual looking to diversify research experience prior to graduate school or beginning a career.
 The pay rate is $20.81/hour for candidates with a bachelor’s degree. Compensation will not be given for higher degrees.  The preferred start date is December 2026, but other start dates will be considered. This 12-month position could be extended for an additional year depending on funding (2 years maximum).
 Field Technician, BA/BS (Oswego Biological Station in Oswego, NY): 
This individual will work as part of a team and support research associated with scientific surveys conducted on the R/V Kaho (70’ vessel) and small vessels (<26’) working out of Oswego, NY.
The position requires living and working aboard a rocking vessel for periods of up to 12 days, lifting 50 pounds, and working in adverse weather conditions during the day and night.
Laboratory work includes fish age interpretation, data management, video habitat characterization and other sample processing.
This contractor must pass a no cost pre-employment physical, enroll in a random drug testing program and be able to obtain a personal passport or enhanced driver’s license for work in Canada.
Field gear is provided, and travel will be paid for.
 Applicants should have an interest in assisting with field work aboard both small and large vessels and be familiar with core scientific practices, including following protocols, recording data, and analyzing results. Experience operating small vessels and fabricating or repairing laboratory equipment is preferred. Familiarity with data management tools or experience using R is also beneficial.
 To apply send an email to Scott Stahl (sstahl@usgs.gov) with the subject line “Student Contractor Position” and attach your cover letter, resume/CV, unofficial transcripts, and contact information for 1-2 references. Applications will be accepted until 10/16/26.
 Student Service Contract Specifics

Under the Student Services Program, USGS contracts directly with the students and students must be at least 18 years of age.

Former students who graduated more than 12 months ago or left school without graduating are not eligible for this program.

Students are not Federal Employees. They are self-employed and therefore required to report and pay their own taxes and social security. They will be issued a 1099 form.

USGS employees, their spouses and children are not eligible to participate in this program.

The total duration for the contract shall not exceed two calendar years.

Student hourly rates are adjusted each calendar year that Federal Employees receive a cost of living adjustment.

The pay rate is commensurate with the statement of work, not the level of education. Students who have more years of study than required are not necessarily paid at a higher rate than required by the work statement.

Contractors are paid only for hours worked, with no holiday or annual leave benefits. Contractors can work more than 8 hours a day or 40 hours per week, however they get paid the same amount for each hour worked (i.e., no overtime pay rate).

Contractors are entitled to one hour of paid sick leave for every 30 hours worked.

Students must obtain a UEI (Unique Entity Identifier) number and register in SAM (System for award management (sam.gov)) before a contract can be issued to them. Be aware this service is free. If you are asked for payment, you are not at the right site. Documentation will be provided to make the SAM process easier.

Non-US citizens may be eligible to participate, depending on their immigration status and applicable regulations of the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Service (formerly Immigration and Naturalization Service).

Description: The Fish Connections Lab at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is seeking a highly motivated M.S. student for a graduate assistantship(s) (stipend plus tuition covered, may include teaching) beginning in Fall 2027. The successful applicant will develop a thesis project focused on the ecology, evolution, and/or conservation of reef fish symbioses. There may be multiple topics addressed within this project, including animal ecology, disturbance ecology, morphology, behavior, dietary ecology, community ecology, genomics, microbiome, and/or habitat use. The Fish Connections Lab works on a variety of reef fish symbioses globally, for example clownfish-anemone, goby-coral, and cleaner-client-habitat mutualisms. Studying these symbioses often incorporates field, aquaria, and laboratory techniques. Students will receive training in study design, field and laboratory techniques, and data analysis. Students will be expected to present at scientific conferences and publish their research in peer-reviewed journals. The successful applicant will begin their M.S. program in August 2027.

Rio Grande Valley is a vibrant, multicultural community with an affordable cost of living and year-round warm weather.

Applicants should be highly motivated, capable of conducting fieldwork under challenging conditions, able to manage multiple projects, and willing to work both independently and collaboratively. Applicants should be comfortable participating in field collections, euthanasia, and preservation of specimens. Competitive applicants will demonstrate intellectual curiosity, initiative, strong organizational skills, and excellent written and oral communication. Students must have the ability to travel for many weeks away (possibly in remote places with limited connection) and travel overseas. Highly competitive applicants will demonstrate experience conducting field research (underwater experience is a bonus), preferably during their undergraduate program, and other research engagement. Southeastern Louisiana University’s College of Science and Technology in Hammond, Louisiana, invites applications for Department Head for the Department of Biological Sciences. This position, which is a 12-month appointment, is responsible for the planning, direction, and development of the department as well as budget management. The Department Head is expected to provide strategic leadership for curriculum development, implementation of a modern pedagogy, and assessment of student learning. The Department Head is the driving force behind the development and enhancement of research programs, scholarly efforts, as well as strategic initiatives that focus on recruitment and retention issues. This position will engage in teaching undergraduate and graduate courses and will be encouraged to maintain a research program appropriate in a department with both an undergraduate and Master’s degree program. This twelve-month position, which is not term-limited, is primarily responsible for advancing the culture of academic distinction where excellence in teaching, research, scholarship, and service is expected.

Southeastern Louisiana University is located in Hammond, approximately 50 miles from the metropolitan centers of New Orleans and Baton Rouge. Southeastern has an enrollment of more than 15,000 students and the Department of Biological Sciences has approximately 650 undergraduate majors and 30 graduate students, in 6 concentrations: Ecology, Environmental, & Evolutionary Biology; Integrative Biology; Microbiology & Molecular Biology; Plant Science; Biology Education; and Business.

A successful candidate will demonstrate a commitment to advancing the department's mission and have a proven track record of academic leadership or related experience, budget management, and fostering research and academic excellence. Specifically, some key responsibilities are:

1. Lead and provide representation for faculty, staff and students in Biological Sciences.

2. Oversee strategic (includes short- and long-range) planning, direction, and development of the academic department.

3. Coordinate and administer the rules and academic standards regarding undergraduate and graduate instruction, curricula, and scheduling for the department.

4. Plan and initiate programs concerning organizational, operational, and academic functions for the department and oversee their execution.

5. Lead faculty development and recruitment for the department. Evaluate faculty in accordance with evaluation guidelines and the guidelines for tenure and promotion. Make recommendations for faculty appointments, promotions, and compensation. Provide support for and assist the department in fundraising, proposal writing, and developing new programs in congruence with the mission of Southeastern Louisiana University.

6. Manage and allocate the department's budget to effectively support academic, research, and operational needs. Develop budget requests that are forwarded to the Deans.

7. Coordinate policies and procedures for the department.

8. Represent the department at formal functions and in public relations efforts such as speaking engagements and outreach activities in the community.

9. Work with and chair University committees as assigned. Assist the Dean in the formulation of college policies and procedures.

10. Maintain operational procedures, rules, and standards relating to faculty and staff.

11. Oversee the scheduling of courses and recommend the implementation and removal of courses, concentrations, and programs.

12 Advise the Dean and the Provost on academic matters concerning the department.

13. Lead efforts in the assessment of student learning outcomes and program effectiveness.

14. Champion the growth and enhancement of research initiatives, seeking opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration and external funding.

15. Assume responsibility for buildings and their maintenance, oversight of departmental purchases, and inventory.

Questions concerning this position should be directed to Dr. Christopher Murray, Chair of the Department Head Screening Committee, at cmurray@selu.edu. Please apply through the University employment site (https://ulsselu.wd503.myworkdayjobs.com/SLU) by November 8th 2026. Doctorate in a discipline of Biological Sciences from an accredited university by hire date.
Credentials that warrant appointment at the academic rank of Associate Professor or Professor.

experiences.

Description
The Oklahoma Biological Survey (OBS) and the School of Biological Sciences (SBS) at the University of Oklahoma (OU) invite applications for a full-time tenure-track Assistant Professor position in Vector Biology and One Health science with a starting date of August 16, 2027, teaching 1 course per academic year.
 We seek an innovative, collaborative, and forward-looking colleague with a record of research in vector biology, whose research addresses the biological foundations of One Health and the effects of environmental change on arthropods of medical/veterinary importance and/or vector-borne diseases; who will establish a nationally recognized, student-engaged, interdisciplinary, and externally funded research program; and who will build collaborations across the University and with public, agricultural, wildlife, and health partners, and contribute to the University’s efforts to understand and respond to emerging health challenges associated with environmental and land-use as part of OU’s Lead On Strategic Plan.
 Areas of interest for the ideal candidate include, but are not limited to the following: vector biodiversity and population and range dynamics, vector-host-pathogen interactions, medical and veterinary entomology, and disease ecology. We are especially interested in candidates who integrate field-based investigation with molecular, genomic, geospatial, quantitative, or predictive approaches to address questions related to vectors and vector-borne disease in the context of One Health.
 The successful candidate will be expected to: (1) develop and sustain an extramurally-funded research program; (2) contribute to statewide biodiversity monitoring and environmental health surveillance through the Oklahoma Biological Survey; (3) foster interdisciplinary collaborations across OU and with governmental, tribal, agricultural, wildlife, and public-health partners; (4) mentor undergraduate and graduate students in research and experiential learning; and (5) contribute to undergraduate and graduate teaching in areas such as vector biology, vector–host–pathogen interactions, parasitology, medical and veterinary entomology and/or microbiology, microbial genetics, and One Health science.
 The OBS is both a state agency and a research unit in the Dodge Family College of Arts and Sciences affiliated with the School of Biological Sciences at OU, and is home to the Robert Bebb Herbarium, the Oklahoma Natural Heritage Inventory, and the Oklahoma Natural Areas Registry program. The SBS was recently established through the integration of the departments of Biology and Microbiology and Plant Biology to align graduate programs and research with faculty strengths and OU’s Lead On Strategic Plan.
OU invests in its faculty by providing support and resources through the Center for Faculty Excellence and Vice President for Research and Partnerships Office. The Dodge Family College of Arts and Sciences supports faculty development through senior faculty mentoring, new faculty orientation series, and access to research and educational support. We encourage candidates to apply who seek to contribute to collegial and interdisciplinary research environments.

Qualifications
Required Qualifications:
Ph.D. in biological sciences, vector biology, or other related fields.
Established record of high-quality research and publications.
Demonstrated record of, or clear potential for, strong extramural funding.
Demonstrated or explicit commitment to outreach, community engagement, and service to the OBS, SBS, university, and discipline.
Familiarity with effective teaching practices and student mentoring approaches

Preferred Qualifications:
Experience leading collaborative projects and working with interdisciplinary teams.
Demonstrated teaching and mentoring record, evidenced by list of courses taught, description of innovative pedagogy, effective student mentoring and engagement, and/or a history of positive student and peer evaluations.
Demonstrated potential for coordination and collaboration development with state offices, tribal organizations, private landowners, and the communities of OBS, SBS, and OU.

Application Instructions
Applicants are required to submit: 1) a cover letter (limited to 2 pages) describing your motivations and qualifications for applying and fit with the OBS and one or more of the SBS research themes; 2) a full curriculum vitae; and 3) a statement of interest (limited to 4 pages) that includes a (i) brief summary of your current and future scholarship, (ii) brief summary of your experience with classroom teaching and mentoring, and advising undergraduate and graduate students, and (iii) brief discussion of your taxonomic expertise as it relates to your research program. Applications must be submitted online via Interfolio at https://apply.interfolio.com/193462. Additionally, applicants must submit contact information within Interfolio to initiate requests for three (3) confidential letters of recommendation; all letters must be on file for an application to be reviewed for the position. Please limit the cover letter and statement of interest to a maximum of 2 and 4 pages, respectively. Additional materials may be requested.

Screening of candidates will begin October 19, 2026 and will continue until the position is filled.

We encourage applications from veterans, women, persons of color, indigenous peoples, persons with disabilities and other individuals who can contribute to our intellectual diversity and cultural richness.

Research Project: This project evaluates potential modifications of infrastructure aimed at reducing bat fatalities at energy facilities.  Two species of bats will be evaluated.  Both species are forest-obligate species found on all National Forests.  They are also the 2 species most frequently killed via energy infrastructure.  The research involves observational studies of bats interactions with infrastructure as well as capture of individuals that are observed in choice experiments conducted in the field. Results will be shared through publications and presentations to energy developers and forest managers considering energy infrastructure installations on their lands.  

We have an opportunity for a fellow to be a part of this learning experience in the construction of experimental apparatus in the field, capture and handle bats, conduct choice experiments with captured bats, deploy and monitor audio and video recordings, process resulting data streams, and analyze these data. This will be conducted in Humboldt County, California and includes opportunities to interact with a wide range of collaborators including academics, government employees, community members, university students, and energy industry representatives.

Detail how energy infrastructure can affect bat behavior and contribute to bat fatalities.
Develop an understanding of the ecology and conservation needs of two forest-obligate bat species commonly affected by energy facilities.
Preform safe, ethical techniques for capturing, handling, and releasing bats during field-based choice experiments.
Conduct behavioral observations and controlled choice experiments with bats in natural settings.

o   1 UF technician: timeline Nov - June

 The Game Lab at UF and the Fish and Wildlife Research Institute (FWRI) of FWC are recruiting 3 research technicians for a collaborative Osceola wild turkey ecology research project in south-central Florida. 
 Fieldwork will be located on private property near Melbourne, FL. Shared housing (no pets) will be provided on-site in the form of a fieldhouse as well as field vehicles will be provided. The successful candidates will work under the guidance of a master's student serving as trapping coordinator, alongside other UF and FWC personnel. Focus of the project will be on various aspects of turkey trapping fieldwork including but not limited to: organizing and preparing trapping equipment, scouting and baiting trap sites, trapping and tagging wild turkeys with rocket nets, tracking and downloading data from tagged turkeys, entering data, vegetation sampling, and monitoring nests and broods. Field conditions include inclement weather, both hot and cold temperatures, high humidity, biting insects, and occasional wet conditions. These positions are primarily field work based (~100%).

 Due to the highly dynamic nature of live-capture operations, the applicant must be able to work an extremely flexible schedule with possible weekend shifts and consistently work early mornings. The applicants must be able to work well in a team setting and get along well with others as the chosen candidates will live alongside coworkers in close quarters. Technicians will work in a team setting during capture season (Dec-Feb). The long-term technician will continue to work alongside the master’s student during monitoring season (Feb-June). 

 Qualifications: Applicants preferably should have a background in wildlife biology and field research and are working toward or have completed a B.S. in Wildlife Biology, Forestry, or a related field.
Successful candidates will be expected to have field experience with (1) animal trapping and handling with preference given to applicants with experience in wild turkey trapping and rocket netting, (2) blood draws/bleeding birds, (3) radio telemetry and tracking/triangulating wildlife, (4) operating 4WD vehicles, landscaping tools, and navigation tools including GPS and maps. Applicants must tolerate harsh environmental conditions and work early mornings, long days, late nights, and weekends when necessary. A valid U.S. driver’s license is required.
 To Apply: Applications will be reviewed as they are received, so applicants are encouraged to apply early. Applications should be sent prior to October 16th, 2026. Applications received later than this date may still be considered only if the positions have yet to be filled.

If interested in applying, please send a single combined PDF with the subject line title “Osceola_research_technician_lastname_firstname” to Cole Carter (michaelcarter1@ufl.edu). including:

(1)  A cover letter summarizing your qualifications for the position. This should also highlight whether you wish to be considered for the short-term or long-term position, or both. The letter can be addressed to the ‘UF Turkey Research Group’.
(2)  CV/resume
(3)  Contact information for 3 references


Note:  The Dec – Feb and Nov - June UF roles will be working in Dr. Marcus Lashley’s lab in the Wildlife Ecology and Conservation department at UF and the Dec – Feb trapping technician will be working under the gamebird research biologist at the FWRI with FWC. All of the technician roles will be working under 1 collaborative project that will be coordinated by the graduate student Cole Carter on a day-to-day basis. 

The UF GAME Lab and FWRI are committed to increasing the diversity of science and scientists, and we encourage applicants from underrepresented groups in STEM to apply
